strengths: Well-motivated reformulation of HMER as discrete diffusion addresses concrete problems (exposure bias, structural inconsistency) in autoregressive approaches with clear problem decomposition
Symbol-aware tokenization elegantly solves the technical problem of LaTeX's discontinuous edits violating local denoising assumptions through symbol-modifier decomposition
Rigorous experimental methodology: careful cross-dataset evaluation, reimplemented baselines at standardized resolution, proper evaluation protocols (LgEval for CROHME), results averaged over 10 runs
Strong empirical results achieving state-of-the-art on MathWriting (5.56% CER, 60.42% EM) with consistent improvements across four CROHME editions (2014-2023)
Comprehensive analysis including thorough ablation studies, output diversity analysis revealing model explores plausible alternatives under ambiguity, and Syntax Error Rate tracking
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and well-structured methodology section
weaknesses: Severe inference efficiency limitation: main configuration achieves only 0.62 FPS vs. 1.6-1.77 FPS for baselines (~2.7× slower); while mentioned, this critical practical constraint is dramatically understated given deployment implications

Critical missing comparison with NAMER [11], the most closely related work addressing exposure bias via non-autoregressive modeling; no ablation comparing diffusion vs. single-step NAR decoding despite NAMER's relevance

Limited methodological novelty: discrete diffusion from Sahoo et al. (2024), symbol-aware tokenization is straightforward feature engineering, RMML is standard mutual learning with KL divergence—main contribution is application engineering rather than algorithmic innovation

Unclear technical specifications: modifier embedding extraction from LaTeX not algorithmically specified, inference procedure for ambiguous inputs producing multiple outputs not clarified (argmax? ensemble?), parameter count 28M vs. 6-7M for baselines (4-5× increase) not adequately justified
Missing failure analysis: no discussion of failure modes, specific structural errors, or performance breakdown; alternative parses shown as feature but semantic validity not rigorously evaluated
Incomplete statistical analysis: results averaged over 10 runs but no confidence intervals, significance tests, or standard deviations reported, limiting strength of improvement claims
Architectural confound: ViT encoder differs from CNN-based encoders in baselines; unclear if improvements stem from diffusion formulation or encoder choice
Domain-specific design: symbol-aware tokenization inherently specific to mathematical expressions with LaTeX syntax; limited discussion of generalization to other structured recognition tasks
Reproducibility concerns: no code release mentioned, sparse training details (optimization, learning rates, diffusion schedule), insufficient specificity on modifier embedding computation

strengths: Novel application of masked diffusion to HMER with well-motivated problem formulation addressing exposure bias in AR models and limitations of NAR approaches
Clever domain-specific design: Symbol-Aware Tokenization elegantly solves the locality problem inherent to diffusion over hierarchical LaTeX structures
Strong empirical results: achieves 5.51% CER and 59.9% EM on MathWriting, consistently outperforming all reimplemented baselines with fair experimental setup

Comprehensive experimental validation including step-wise analysis (Fig. 3), ablation studies (Table 3), accuracy-latency trade-offs (Table 4), and error recovery analysis demonstrating gradual refinement dynamics
Enables length-independent computational control through diffusion step count T, providing explicit accuracy-latency trade-off not available in AR methods
Transparent discussion of limitations (data hunger, latency, input resolution) and honest characterization of when the approach is/isn't applicable
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and comprehensive related work positioning
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: masked diffusion and iterative refinement are established techniques; application to HMER is novel but the core innovation is incremental

Significant data hunger (630k samples: 230k + 400k synthetic) with explicit acknowledgment that CROHME-only training is insufficient, undermining cross-dataset generalization claims and practical applicability

Design choices lack rigorous justification: linear diffusion schedule used without comparison to alternatives; T=50 not validated through hyperparameter exploration; RMML loss weights (Eq. 2) appear arbitrary with no ablation on coefficients

Incomplete baseline comparisons: NAMER (key NAR competitor) only reported with literature scores, not reimplemented in matched setting; Uni-MuMER mentioned but not experimentally compared; mask-predict comparison limited

SAT analysis oversimplified: alignment rules (e.g., 'leftmost symbol') lack formal justification; no analysis of failure modes for deeply nested expressions or non-standard LaTeX constructs; no ablation comparing to naive syntax validation

Statistical rigor concerns: no confidence intervals or significance testing; all averages over 10 runs without variance analysis; comparisons with literature-reported baselines marked (*) without error bars

Experimental details incomplete: synthetic data composition in MathWriting not disclosed; training time and convergence behavior not reported; ViT initialization details missing; Fig. 4 error recovery anomaly (CER spike with SAT at t≈20) not explained

Computational overhead not fully contextualized: T=50 achieves 2.5× speedup over CoMER but requires 50 decoder passes; T=10 (73.7 FPS) vs ICAL (7.95 FPS, 6.03% CER) shows modest practical advantage doesn't justify added complexity
Lack of theoretical grounding: paper provides intuition but limited formal justification for why masked diffusion reduces exposure bias specifically for mathematical expression parsing
Reproducibility gaps: no code availability mentioned; missing hyperparameter sensitivity analysis; insufficient details on how RMML-learned consistency transfers to inference
